newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London ended a dull day little changed with interest on the December/March spread. December added 30 cents to close at $304.00, while March was 20 cents higher at $303.50. Raw sugar futures in New York fell through nearby support at 10.40 cents/lb to 10.37 cents/lb basis the March contract. May lost 6 points to close at 10.49 cents/lb. The outer months lost between 1 and 7 seven points.

Fund selling put the market under pressure. Forecasts by London trade house C. Czarnikow of another surplus 1996/97 should have no great impact on prices, as the figures are in line with expectations.

C. CZARNIKOW - World sugar output is expected to total 124.33 million tonnes, raw value, in 1996/97 (crop years), up from the 123.19 million tonnes produced the previous year, C. Czarnikow said. In its second estimate of the world balance, Czarnikow said consumption in 1997 (calendar year) was expected to reach 120.57 million tonnes, 2.24 million tonnes up on 1996.

The company emphasized that not all of the difference between the two will carry through to a stock adjustment because of unrecorded disappearances. Czarnikow said it had raised its 1996/97 disappearance factor by 100,000 tonnes to 750,000 tonnes. This indicated that world sugar stocks would increase by some 3.0 million tonnes after a rise of 4.21 million tonnes in 1995/96, it said.

The company emphasized that although there has been increasing interaction between local markets and the world market in recent years, the sugar sector is far from a homogenous whole. There has been a variety of local and regional situations which have developed influences on prices at different times and this pattern is likely to continue over the coming year, it was added.

UKRAINE - Sugar production in 1996/97 will be lower than had been expected at the beginning of the season and is now estimated at 2.830 million tonnes, raw value, down from 3.793 million tonnes produced in 1995/96. It was warned that the area sown to beet could decline next season because the crop is no longer profitable.

Ukrainian officials also deplored that the Russian Foreign Trade Ministry has sent an order to the government setting white sugar imports at 1.5 million tonnes per year with an Ukrainian allowance of 1.15 million tonnes. Russian sources said that the quota, which had been under consideration for a number of months, was temporary and gave Russian producers a chance to get used to competition.

It was not said when the quota, which must be approved by the government, would be introduced and how long it would remain in place. Ukrainian sugar industry officials pointed out that under the old regime Russia normally got up to 4 million tonnes of white sugar from the Ukraine per year. In 1995 the Ukraine shipped 1.6 million tonnes of its 1.9 million tonnes of refined sugar exports to Russia.
The Russian import quota will put the Ukrainian sugar industry under pressure, as Ukrainian sugar is not competitive internationally. Hence, the industry is dependent on CIS markets.

AUSTRALIA - Sugar exports in September 1997 amounted to 515,826 tonnes, raw value, up on last year's 493,088 tonnes. This brought cumulative exports in the first four months of 1996/97 (June/September) up to 2.08 million tonnes against 1.75 million tonnes in 1995/96. Total exports in 1995/96 reached 4.17 million tonnes against 4.48 million tonnes in 1994/95 and 3.55 million tonnes in 1993/94.

Major countries of destination in June/September 1996 were Canada with 395,479 tonnes raws against 288,941 tonnes, South Korea with 319,075 tonnes, up from 259,452 tonnes, Malaysia with 303,058 tonnes against 306,872 tonnes and Japan with 199,090 tonnes, down from 296,936 tonnes. Australia continues to be a substantial exporter of white sugar, although the tonnages shipped in 1996 are below those seen in 1995.

Total white sugar exports in June/September 1996 amounted to 72,347 tonnes, down from last year's 79,321 tonnes. The major countries of destination in 1996 were New Zealand with 26,474 tonnes, Sri Lanka with 19,500 tonnes and Hong Kong with 10,624 tonnes.
